passage: I'm Kavitha, Ankita's neighbour, and my balcony looks over our stairs. Last week Ankita still gripped the railing with both fists and sat down hard after two steps. Today she let go, bent her knees, wobbled, and walked four quick steps to the bottom stair, then climbed it on hands and knees. Her brother Nikhil clapped so loudly that she toppled onto her bottom. She looked at him, laughed, and pushed herself up again. I can't say what she was thinking, but she didn't look scared.

qa.q: How many steps did Ankita walk after letting go of the railing?
qa.a: She walked four quick steps to the bottom stair.

qa.q: What does Ankita's laugh after toppling suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt safe and amused rather than scared, happy enough to push herself up and try again.

qa.q: How could Nikhil support Ankita's next attempts on the stairs?
qa.a: He could cheer a little more softly and stay close to the stairs, so she can practise climbing without being startled.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see Ankita's progress from the balcony?
qa.a: Kavitha notices a clear change from last week, but admits not knowing exactly what Ankita was thinking.

grounding: Shows a toddler's large-muscle coordination growing from gripping a railing to walking and climbing a step.

passage:
Crèche note, Tuesday
Deepak ate his dal-rice with the spoon today and only needed help with the last few bites. At snack time he picked up single peas between thumb and finger, very slowly, and posted them into his mouth. His cousin Lalit, from the older group, built him a tower of three blocks. Deepak added a fourth, then knocked it all down, squealing. Lalit groaned, then built it again. Tomorrow I'll put out the big wooden beads for threading. 🙂
Ms Anjali

qa.q: What did Deepak pick up between thumb and finger at snack time?
qa.a: He picked up single peas between thumb and finger.

qa.q: What does Deepak's squeal suggest about how he felt about the tower?
qa.a: He added a fourth block, knocked it all down and squealed, which shows he felt delighted and excited.

qa.q: What small step would help Deepak keep practising with his fingers at home?
qa.a: His family could offer small, soft finger foods and let him feed himself, even if it's slow and messy.

qa.q: What is it like for Lalit when Deepak knocks the tower down?
qa.a: Lalit is a bit fed up at first and groans, but still cares enough to build it again for a younger cousin.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler refining small hand movements: using a spoon, picking up peas with thumb and finger, and stacking blocks.

passage:
Monday: Sabina leaned to reach her ball and tipped straight over onto the rug. Her big sister Rekha grabbed for her sleeve too late.
Thursday: Sabina squatted to pick up the ball, swayed, and flung one hand out to the sofa. She stayed up. Rekha cheered from the doorway.
The next Sunday: Sabina ran after the ball, stumbled on the rug's edge, caught herself on both hands, then stood and kept running. Rekha only looked up from her book and smiled.

qa.q: What did Sabina grab to stay up on Thursday?
qa.a: She flung one hand out to the sofa.

qa.q: What might Sabina have felt when she caught herself and kept running on Sunday?
qa.a: She probably felt confident and happy, because she stood straight up and carried on chasing the ball instead of stopping.

qa.q: How could a parent help Sabina keep building her balance?
qa.a: They could give her safe space to squat, climb low steps and chase balls, staying near without catching her every time.

qa.q: Why might Rekha react differently on Sunday than on Monday?
qa.a: By Sunday Rekha has seen Sabina catch herself, so she trusts her little sister more and no longer needs to rush over.

grounding: Shows a toddler's core strength and balance improving over several days until she can catch herself when she stumbles.

passage:
Note for Ojas's Papa, from Nani, Saturday
Before lunch Ojas patted his tummy and said "mum-mum", so he knows when he's hungry now. After lunch he rubbed his eyes and dragged his blanket to me, and he went down for his nap without a fuss. Earlier he'd stopped playing, held his nappy and fussed; he needed changing. His cousin Suraj kept wanting to play trains and sulked when Ojas lay down, so I let Suraj choose the nap-time story. 🙂

qa.q: What did Ojas drag to Nani after lunch?
qa.a: He dragged his blanket to her.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he rubbed his eyes?
qa.a: He was tired and sleepy, and bringing his blanket showed he knew he wanted rest.

qa.q: How could Nani keep helping Ojas notice his body's signals?
qa.a: She could name each signal out loud, like "you're hungry" or "you're sleepy", whenever he shows it.

qa.q: What is it like for Suraj when Ojas lies down for his nap?
qa.a: Suraj feels disappointed to lose a playmate, but choosing the story helps Suraj feel included.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler beginning to recognise hunger, tiredness and a wet nappy and signal them to a caregiver.

passage:
Playgroup note, Wednesday
Himani still says only "ba" and "ma", but she understands far more. When I said, "Bring me your shoes," she toddled to the rack, brought one shoe, then went back for the second. At clean-up I asked her to put the duck in the basket, and she did. At pickup her brother Ojas asked, "Himani, where's your bag?" She pointed straight at the hook. Ojas stared. "She knows!" I'll keep giving her short, clear requests. 😊
Teacher Shobha

qa.q: What did Himani do when Teacher Shobha asked for her shoes?
qa.a: She toddled to the rack, brought one shoe, then went back for the second.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when she pointed at the hook for Ojas?
qa.a: She likely felt proud and pleased to show she understood, even though she can't say the words yet.

qa.q: How could Himani's family build on what she understands?
qa.a: They could give her short, clear requests and name objects as she touches them, then wait for her to show she understood.

qa.q: Why was Ojas surprised at pickup?
qa.a: Ojas probably thought his little sister couldn't understand much because she barely talks, so her quick pointing surprised him.

grounding: Shows a toddler who cannot yet speak much understanding words and following simple instructions.

passage: I'm Rajni, and I sell vegetables at the gate of Sabina's building. For months Sabina just babbled at me, "ba-ba-da", and pointed. This morning she tugged her Ammi's dupatta, looked at my basket and said, "Mango. Want mango." Her cousin Farhan, holding her other hand, shouted, "Two words!" and asked her to say it again. She did, louder, and held out both hands. I can't know what went on in that little head, but she wasn't pointing anymore.

qa.q: What did Sabina say when she looked at the basket?
qa.a: She said, "Mango. Want mango."

qa.q: What does Sabina holding out both hands suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt eager and pleased, confident that her words would get her the mango.

qa.q: How could Sabina's family encourage her new words?
qa.a: They could answer her words quickly and repeat them back a little longer, like "You want a mango? Here's a mango."

qa.q: How does Farhan react to Sabina's new words?
qa.a: Farhan is thrilled and wants to hear it again, as if the two words are a big event for the whole family.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler moving from babbling and pointing to a short sentence that asks for what she wants.

passage: In their small flat in Copenhagen, Emil sat on the floor while his sister Noa pushed a wooden train into a cardboard tunnel. Emil's eyes followed it right to the tunnel's mouth. When it vanished, he didn't look at Noa's hand. He turned his head to the far end and waited, mouth open. The train rolled out. Emil shrieked and slapped the rug. "Again!" Noa laughed. "He knows where it comes out now," she called to their dad.

qa.q: What did Noa push into the cardboard tunnel?
qa.a: She pushed a wooden train into the cardboard tunnel.

qa.q: Why did Emil turn his head to the far end of the tunnel?
qa.a: He expected the train to come out there and waited eagerly; when it did, he was delighted.

qa.q: What game could Emil's dad try next to build on this?
qa.a: He could roll a ball behind the sofa and let Emil guess which side it will come out.

qa.q: What is it like for Noa to watch Emil wait at the far end?
qa.a: Noa is amused and a little proud, noticing that her little brother has learned something new and wanting their dad to see it.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a moving toy with his eyes and anticipating where it will reappear.

passage:
Note for Thomas's mum, Friday
Today I hid his toy car under the blue blanket while he watched. Last month he'd just look away. Today Thomas pulled the blanket off at once and held up the car. Then his cousin Sonali hid it under a cushion instead. Thomas lifted the blanket first, frowned, and started patting the other cushions until he found it. Sonali clapped and hid it again. I'll try two cups and a ball next week.
Grace (nanny)

qa.q: Where did Sonali hide the toy car?
qa.a: Sonali hid it under a cushion.

qa.q: What does Thomas's frown suggest when the car wasn't under the blanket?
qa.a: It suggests he was puzzled and a little frustrated, but sure the car was still somewhere, so he kept searching.

qa.q: How could Grace build on Thomas's searching?
qa.a: Grace could play the two-cups-and-a-ball game, hiding the ball while Thomas watches and letting him find it.

qa.q: How does Sonali seem to feel about the hiding game?
qa.a: Sonali seems to enjoy it, clapping when Thomas finds the car and eager to hide it again.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler understanding that a covered toy still exists and searching for it.

passage:
Daycare note, Monday
Minakshi arrived quiet today, but her brother Kishore stayed a few minutes at drop-off and blew bubbles for her. Every time one popped on her nose, she squealed, kicked her legs and reached for the next. When he pretended to sneeze bubbles, she laughed so hard she fell sideways on the mat, then sat up asking "more!" Kishore looked very pleased with himself. I've added bubbles to our morning songs. 😊
Aunty Lata

qa.q: What did Kishore blow for Minakshi at drop-off?
qa.a: He blew bubbles for her.

qa.q: How can you tell Minakshi felt delighted by the bubbles?
qa.a: She squealed, kicked her legs, laughed hard and asked for more, which shows real joy and excitement.

qa.q: How could Aunty Lata keep Minakshi's mornings playful?
qa.a: She could keep bubbles in the morning songs and add other gentle surprises, like peek-a-boo or silly sounds.

qa.q: What is it like for Kishore to make his sister laugh?
qa.a: Kishore feels proud and pleased, because his pretend sneeze got the biggest laugh of all.

grounding: Shows a toddler's delight and laughter in response to playful bubbles.

passage:
Day one: Hemant, strapped into his pram at the market, arched his back and screamed when he couldn't reach the bananas. His cousin Ujjwal covered both ears.
Day four: Strapped in again, Hemant kicked and yelled, "Out!" His Mummy said, "You're angry. Two more shops, then you walk." He still grumbled.
Day ten: When the straps clicked, Hemant scowled and asked, "Walk later?" Ujjwal handed him a banana to hold, and he rode quietly to the last shop.

qa.q: What did Hemant ask when the straps clicked on day ten?
qa.a: He scowled and asked, "Walk later?"

qa.q: Why did Hemant scream on day one?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and angry because the straps stopped him from reaching the bananas he wanted.

qa.q: Which part of Mummy's approach helped Hemant, and why?
qa.a: Naming his anger and telling him exactly when he could walk gave him something to wait for, so his protests got smaller. 👍

qa.q: How does Ujjwal's reaction change across the days?
qa.a: Ujjwal first covers both ears at the screaming, but by day ten is calm enough to help by handing Hemant a banana.

grounding: Shows a toddler's frustration at being held in a pram when he wants something, and how it softens over days.
